analysis.one_liner: Bans companies from using personal health data for advertising and gives people the right to see and delete it.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in August 2022, referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, and received no further action or vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for companies to use people's personally-identifiable health data — from fitness trackers, web browsing, medical records, or any other source — to target them with ads, with an exception for public health campaigns. It would give individuals the right to access the health data companies hold about them and to have it deleted, within 45 days and for free. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the rules, and individuals could sue violators for at least $1,000 per violating ad, plus attorney's fees.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people whose health information — from fitness trackers, web searches, and health apps — is currently collected and sold to target ads. They would gain a legal right to see and delete that data and to sue companies that misuse it. People with sensitive conditions like mental illness or reproductive health needs would face less risk of their health status being inferred and used for advertising.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People whose health data gets mined

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for companies to use personally-identifiable health data — including data from fitness trackers, web browsing, and medical centers — for commercial advertising.
Gives individuals the right to access their health data that companies hold, in a readable format, and to request its deletion, with no fee and a 45-day compliance deadline.
Lets the FTC enforce the ban and lets individuals sue violators, with at least $1,000 in damages per violating advertisement and attorney's fees.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that collect health data on 1,000 or more people per year — data brokers, advertisers, apps, and websites — would lose the ability to profit from health-based ad targeting and would bear the cost of building access and deletion systems, plus FTC enforcement and private lawsuits.

drawbacks.text: The bill covers only health data used in advertising and entities collecting data on 1,000 or more people per year, leaving smaller data collectors and non-advertising uses of health data unregulated.

The bill explicitly preserves HIPAA and does not require companies to collect or retain data they otherwise would not, so the protections layer on top of existing health-privacy rules rather than creating a single unified standard.

Key terms like 'personally-identifiable health data' and 'public health campaign' would be defined later by an FTC rulemaking within 180 days of enactment, leaving the law's real scope uncertain until rules are written.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy benefit is real and the compliance burden on data brokers and ad-tech firms is modest and proportionate, with a limited-scope exemption for legitimate public health campaigns and a right-of-deletion carve-out that avoids forcing companies to keep data longer than they would otherwise. The main drawback is that HIPAA already covers much health data held by doctors and insurers, so the new protection reaches mainly the data those rules miss — a genuine gap, but one where the bill's full practical reach would have depended on FTC rulemaking that never had to be judged.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in August 2022 and never moved, so it expired when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Klobuchar, joined by Senator Whitehouse, introduced the bill on August 2, 2022.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day.
No committee hearing, markup, or floor vote followed, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that profit from mining and targeting people's health data are better off, since the restrictions never took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Firms mining health data for ads

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban commercial use of health data in advertising.

against.name: Data brokers and ad-tech industry
against.what_they_did: Opposition is not documented in the congressional record; no group is recorded acting against the bill, which received no committee or floor action.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors are Democrats and the bill never reached a vote, so the record shows no cross-party position on it.

industries.note: The bill would bar them from selling or using health data for targeted advertising and expose them to FTC enforcement and private lawsuits, cutting off a profitable use of sensitive personal information.

industries.industry: Digital advertising platforms and app makers
industries.note: Platforms and apps that monetize health and fitness signals through ads would lose that revenue stream, which today is paid for with users' private health information.
